messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 61

At thirty-two, Amir, a South Asian man, has spent the better part of his adulthood working the night shift as a housekeeper for a downtown hotel. The incident happens in late autumn. He is walking home from work, cutting through the narrow passage behind the textile market to save time. A man steps from the shadows, the edge of a blade catching the streetlight before pressing against Amir’s ribs. Words are exchanged in a hurry. Amir hands over his wallet and phone. The man shoves him backward into a damp brick wall, the impact driving the air from his lungs, then melts into the dark. Amir remains on the ground until his breathing slows and the hum of the streetlamps returns. He walks the rest of the way home in silence, his hands trembling only after he unlocks the front door. In the weeks that follow, the quiet of his apartment feels heavier. He wakes at 2 a.m. most nights, his heart hammering against his ribs as if the alley were right behind him. He checks the deadbolt three times before he can close his eyes. When sleep comes, the images return: the glint of metal, the smell of wet pavement, Zara’s voice from the bedroom snapping him awake. He stops leaving after midnight. He tells his wife he prefers to rest through the night, though he actually stares at the ceiling until his eyes burn. At work, the changes are quiet but steady. Amir cleans twelve rooms a day, his routine once a kind of grounding rhythm—strip the linens, polish the mirror, verify the minibar. Now, he counts the seconds between tasks. He walks the perimeter of every hallway before entering a suite, listening for footsteps, noting which doors face the corridor. He avoids the east stairwell; the acoustics mirror the alley’s echo. When a colleague taps his shoulder, his whole body jerks, and he spends the rest of the shift with his shoulders locked tight. His supervisor notices the dropped turnovers and the way Amir flinches at radio static. Amir insists he is fine, just tired. Zara tries to bridge the distance. She leaves extra blankets on the couch, makes his favorite chai, asks about his day. He answers in short sentences, his gaze fixed on the window. He catches himself wondering if she will notice the tremor in his hands, if she will see him as less capable. He begins to dread the intimacy of their bedroom, afraid that closing his eyes will drop him back into that stretch of pavement. He rolls onto his side, facing the wall, and waits for the dawn. On weekends, he drives the long way to the market, even when the traffic is thick. He keeps the windows rolled up and the radio on low. When he hears a car backfire or sees someone walking briskly behind him, his chest tightens and his breath comes in shallow pulls. He tells himself it is paranoia, that he is overreacting, but the body does not wait for permission to brace. He finishes his rounds early, packs his cart, and leaves before the evening shift change. At home, he sits at the kitchen table and watches the streetlights flicker on, one by one, waiting for the house to settle, waiting for his pulse to match the quiet.
